questions.q: What is an Indicator of Compromise (IOC)?
options: A concrete, observable artifact that signals a system or network has likely been compromised
A general risk score assigned to a vendor's security product
A subjective guess an analyst makes without any supporting evidence
A type of firewall rule that blocks all inbound traffic
questions.explain: An IOC is specific enough to match exactly — a file hash, an IP, a registry key — not a hunch or a feeling.

questions.q: Why does a file hash remain a reliable IOC even after malware is renamed and moved to a different folder?
options: A cryptographic hash depends only on the file's exact contents, not its name or location
Hashes are recalculated automatically whenever a file is renamed
Antivirus software ignores filenames entirely and only scans folder paths
File hashes change every time a file is renamed, which is what triggers detection
questions.explain: Because the hash is generated from the file's bytes, the exact same file still produces the exact same hash no matter what it's named or where it's stored.

questions.q: What made a particular domain name famous as a network-level IOC during the 2017 WannaCry ransomware outbreak?
options: The malware checked whether that domain was already registered before encrypting files, and a researcher registering it accidentally triggered a kill switch
It was the personal website of the malware's author
It was the only domain ever blocked by any firewall
It was a domain used exclusively for sending phishing emails
questions.explain: WannaCry's check-before-encrypt logic meant that registering the domain made every future infection see it as already live and stop, an unintentional kill switch.

questions.q: What is a classic example of a registry-based IOC on a Windows system?
options: An entry added under a Windows Run key so malware launches automatically at startup
A change to the system's display resolution setting
A new desktop wallpaper image file
A browser bookmark added by the user
questions.explain: A Run key entry is a classic persistence artifact — it's how malware ensures it keeps launching even after the machine reboots.

questions.q: What pattern would signal an active phishing campaign as an email-based IOC?
options: The same subject line hitting dozens of inboxes in a short window, or a sender display name that doesn't match the real sending domain
An employee receiving exactly one email per day from their manager
A calendar invite sent to a single recipient
An email with no subject line at all
questions.explain: A repeated subject line across many inboxes at once, or a spoofed display name mismatched against the actual sending domain, is how a SOC recognizes a phishing campaign in progress.
